item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=artificial+intelligence+agency+accountability+decision+consequences+responsibility&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Determining Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence-Based Security Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The chapter discusses the determination of who is responsible when artificial intelligence is used for security decision making within complex organizational environments. It looks at how accountability is shared among system designers, vendors, deployers, and human operators when AI-driven tools are used to influence detection actions, prioritization, and response. The chapter investigates legal principles explaining the relationship between control, foreseeability, and duty of care, along with regulatory requirements for human oversight and governance. It also examines issues related to automation bias, black-box models, and extended decision chains that involve Security Operations Centers and third parties. Special focus is given to documentation, role clarity, chain of command for escalation, and auditability as means of defining responsibility. Through combining a legal perspective with security operational practice, the chapter outlines a system for determining responsibility, handling liability, and making defensible decisions in AI-assisted security systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 9]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-3693-4099-8.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence-Driven Corporate Social Responsibility Reporting\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>In a global environment where stakeholders believe ethical company practices, CSR reporting is vital for transparency. Through combining a legal perspective with security operational practice, the chapter outlines a system for determining responsibility, handling liability, and making defensible decisions in AI-assisted security systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 9]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-3693-4099-8.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence-Driven Corporate Social Responsibility Reporting\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>In a global environment where stakeholders believe ethical company practices, CSR reporting is vital for transparency. Traditional reporting methods often fail due to human data management, inaccuracies, and lack of real-time insights. AI has given businesses novel opportunities to rethink CSR strategy and reporting. This chapter examines how AI-driven systems might improve transparency and accountability through automated data gathering, better analytics, and insights that encourage corporate responsibility. It addresses the ethical implications, opportunities, and problems of AI-driven reporting systems and recommends best practices. The chapter discusses case studies of businesses using AI for CSR reporting to boost stakeholder confidence and uphold ethical leadership.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-3693-4099-8.ch007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 22]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.6035/monti.2026.18.01\", \"title\": [\"Traducción sin decisión: la inteligencia artificial y la ilusión de la responsabilidad humana\", \"Translation without decision: artificial intelligence and the illusion of human responsibility\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>La integración de la inteligencia artificial en la traducción no exige únicamente nuevas herramientas o competencias, sino una redefinición sociotécnica de qué entendemos por traducción, agencia y responsabilidad. Esta cuestión no puede resolverse mediante principios éticos abstractos, sino a través de marcos críticos como la gobernanza de los datos, la ética del cuidado y la formación ética del traductor.\\r\\nAl “reciclar” las decisiones traductológicas incorporadas en los datos de entrenamiento y borrar sus contextos y autorías, los sistemas de inteligencia artificial aplicados a la traducción generan una asimetría estructural entre responsabilidad y control. En este artículo argumentamos que para abordar esta asimetría es necesario activar mecanismos de gobernanza que restituyan el factor humano como autoridad que adopta las decisiones. Las implicaciones de este análisis se examinan en relación con la responsabilidad profesional, la ética del cuidado y la formación de traductores, sugiriendo que el futuro de la traducción depende tanto del cumplimiento ético como de la capacidad de recuperar el poder de decisión en entornos mediados por la inteligencia artificial.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.6035/monti.2026.18.01\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 5, 27]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.3389/frai.2026.1800302\", \"title\": [\"Delegated agency and moral responsibility in artificial intelligence\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence ethics is often framed as a response to unprecedented technical autonomy, with risks attributed to recent advances in machine learning and scale. This framing overlooks a recurring ethical structure: the delegation of moral authority to artificial agents. Ethical failures associated with AI are best understood as governance failures rooted in human design choices and accountability arrangements, even where opacity and limited control complicate responsibility attribution.</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\\n                  <jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>A qualitative, interdisciplinary approach integrates historical–thematic analysis, comparative interpretation of technological artifacts, and visual–conceptual synthesis. Mythological figures (Talos, the Golem, Pygmalion), early mechanical automata, and foundational computational systems are analyzed as conceptual models of delegated artificial agency rather than technological precursors.</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\\n                  <jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>Across historical contexts, artificial agents exhibit consistent structural features: bounded autonomy, delegated authority, explicit override mechanisms, and dependence on human oversight. These features directly correspond to contemporary AI ethics concerns, including alignment failures, responsibility gaps, human-in-the-loop control, and system interruptibility.</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\\n                  <jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>The analysis establishes that ethical risk in AI arises from the displacement of human responsibility rather than from machine autonomy. By situating AI within a longer history of artificial agency, the study provides a normative framework that locates moral responsibility unambiguously in human actors and institutions, with direct implications for AI governance and accountability.</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2026.1800302\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 4, 15]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "3e33e366f1498bdafb01633617c9c3c8e0f4bcb9ab1a24800f41da26173860fa", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007", "doi:10.4018/979-8-3693-4099-8.ch007", "doi:10.6035/monti.2026.18.01", "doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1800302"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007", "https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-3693-4099-8.ch007", "https://doi.org/10.6035/monti.2026.18.01", "https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2026.1800302"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
